Euclidean geometry

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Geometry and topology
OurBigBook.com Words: 17k Articles: 318
Euclidean geometry describes flat Euclidean space using lengths, angles, and rigid motions. A coordinate realization uses points x,y∈Rn, Euclidean distance
d(x,y)=∑i=1n​(xi​−yi​)2​,
(1)
and angles determined by the dot product. The coordinate axes are a convenience: translations and rotations change coordinates while preserving these measurements. This makes Euclidean geometry useful for comparing figures and converting measurements along different directions into a single distance.
In the Euclidean plane, through a point outside a line there is exactly one parallel line. This is a standard equivalent formulation of the parallel postulate. Euclid's fifth postulate in the Elements instead describes when two lines meet using the interior angles made by a crossing line.[ref] The assumption has consequences we often take for granted: a triangle's interior angles sum to π, and similar triangles can differ in size while keeping their angles. Comparing with spherical geometry reveals that these are properties of a particular geometry.
As a computed example, the diagonal from (0,0) to (4,3) in a rectangle has length 42+32​=5. The Pythagorean theorem explains why perpendicular contributions add as squares. If the directions cease to meet at a right angle, the law of cosines supplies the missing angle-dependent term. The beauty is that a single distance formula unites geometric constructions, coordinate calculations, and orthogonality in linear algebra.
Make the assumptions visible: in a Cartesian coordinate system with orthogonal axes and the same length unit on each axis, take A=(0,0), B=(4,0) and C=(0,3). The vectors B−A=(4,0) and C−A=(0,3) have dot product zero, establishing a right angle at A before using the Pythagorean theorem. A sketch that merely looks like a right triangle supplies no such guarantee. Likewise, an image stretched horizontally and vertically by different amounts can distort both lengths and angles; a displayed shape and the assumptions defining it must be kept separate.
For a less origin-dependent measurement, take P=(1,2) and Q=(5,5). Their displacement vector is Q−P=(4,3), so their Euclidean distance is again 5. Its Euclidean norm records the direct separation, whereas travelling first horizontally and then vertically covers length 4+3=7. This connects measuring a diagonal to locating two positions from a Cartesian coordinate system. A translation changes where the positions are recorded without changing their separation; a rotation changes the component values without changing the Euclidean norm.

Ray-plane intersection (λ=n⋅rn⋅(a−o)​)

Words: 47 Articles: 1
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
Intersection of o+λr with the plane n⋅(p−a)=0, when n⋅r=0. For a ray, require λ≥0. A zero denominator requires separate parallel or coplanar handling.

Ray-triangle intersection

Words: 20
Ray-plane intersection OurBigBook.com
A ray-plane intersection followed by an inside-triangle test, conveniently using nonnegative barycentric coordinates. Oriented surfaces may additionally require a front-facing hit through back-face culling.

Coplanarity

Words: 47
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
Points are coplanar when they belong to a common plane. For three vectors based at the origin of three-dimensional Euclidean space, this means their span has dimension at most two. Equivalently their scalar triple product, and hence the determinant with those vectors as columns, is zero. This includes dependent or zero vectors.

Geometry in three-dimensional Euclidean space, including volume and surface area.

Napkin ring problem (V=πh3/6)

Words: 71
Solid geometry OurBigBook.com
Removing a central cylindrical hole from a sphere leaves a solid whose volume depends only on its remaining height h. With a=h/2, sphere radius R and hole radius r0​, the rim gives R2−r02​=a2. Every horizontal slice is an annulus of area π(a2−z2), so integrating from −a to a gives V=4πa3/3=πh3/6. This slice equality explains why changing R while retaining h leaves the volume unchanged.

Steinmetz solid

Solid geometry OurBigBook.com
The common region inside equal-radius circular cylinders whose axes meet orthogonally. Two cylinders give a bicylinder; three give a tricylinder.

Bicylinder (V=16a3/3)

Words: 37
Steinmetz solid OurBigBook.com
The solid intersection of two equal-radius infinite circular cylinders whose axes meet at a right angle. For radius a, the cross section at height z along the common perpendicular coordinate is a square of area 4(a2−z2), so its volume is 16a3/3.

Tricylinder (x2+y2≤a2,y2+z2≤a2,z2+x2≤a2)

Words: 79 Articles: 1
Steinmetz solid OurBigBook.com
The common intersection of three equal-radius circular cylinders with mutually perpendicular axes. The displayed inequalities describe a centered example of radius a. It is a Steinmetz solid; its surface area is given by the surface area of a tricylinder formula.
Surface area of a tricylinder (A=24a2(2−2​))
Words: 48
Tricylinder OurBigBook.com
For three radius-a circular cylinders with mutually perpendicular axes through one point, the boundary of their common intersection has three congruent cylindrical surface pieces. On x2+y2=a2, the height restriction is ∣z∣≤amin(∣sinθ∣,∣cosθ∣). Eight congruent sectors give surface area 8a2(2−2​) per piece. Pairwise intersections are curves of zero surface area, so the three pieces add.

Cross-sectional area (A)

Words: 41
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
The area of a planar section through a body. A homogeneous diagonal deformation with transverse stretch ratios λ1​ and λ2​ changes the area of a transverse section from A0​ to A=λ1​λ2​A0​. Cauchy stress tensor components use current cross-sectional area, whereas nominal tractions use reference cross-sectional area.

Geometric scale factor

Words: 34
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
The ratio between corresponding lengths of two geometrically similar figures. Multiplying every length by t>0 multiplies areas by t2 and volumes by t3. For integer-sided triangles, choosing a positive integer scale factor preserves integer side lengths.

Perpendicular lines

Words: 14
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
Two intersecting straight lines are perpendicular if their angle is 90∘. Their direction vectors have zero dot product.

Cone (geometry)

Words: 152 Articles: 1
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A geometric cone joins a fixed point to points of a plane curve by straight lines. A circular cone uses a circle as that curve; its solid version includes the enclosed circular cross-sections. For a right circular cone of height h and base radius R, the cross-section radius varies linearly along the axis, and its volume is πR2h/3 by integration. An elliptic cone allows elliptical cross-sections. The construction differs from the abstract topological cone, which does not specify lengths or angles.

Optimal cylinder inscribed in a cone (xV​=h/3,xA​=h/2)

Words: 77
Cone (geometry) OurBigBook.com
For a coaxial cylinder standing on the base of a right circular cone of height h>0 and semi-vertical angle 0<α<π/2, similar triangles give radius r=(h−x)tanα at cylinder height x. Its volume is V=πx(h−x)2tan2α. Differentiation gives V′=πtan2α(h−x)(h−3x), so the unique positive-volume maximum has x=h/3 and occupies 4/9 of the cone's volume. Its curved surface area is instead A=2πx(h−x)tanα, maximized at x=h/2. Changing the optimized quantity changes the optimal shape, even though the geometric constraint is identical.

Collinearity

Words: 56
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
Points are collinear when they lie on a single line. Two vectors are collinear when their linear span has dimension at most one. For a nonzero vector v, this means that the other vector is λv for some scalar λ. This algebraic convention includes the zero vector; the directional use of “parallel” sometimes assumes both vectors are nonzero.

Quadric surface (xTAx+bTx+c=0)

Words: 673 Articles: 9
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A quadric surface in three-dimensional Euclidean space is the zero set of a real polynomial of degree two. Its quadratic part can be written with a symmetric matrix A, since the antisymmetric matrix part contributes zero to xTAx. An orthogonal diagonalization and a translation expose its geometry: examples include an ellipsoid, an elliptic cone, and a hyperboloid. This affine geometric description allows singular surfaces such as a cone's vertex.

Projective quadric (Q={[v]∈Pn:vTBv=0})

Words: 84
Quadric surface OurBigBook.com
A projective quadric is the zero set of a nonzero homogeneous quadratic polynomial in projective space. Over a field of characteristic different from two, represent it by a symmetric matrix B, up to a nonzero scalar. The gradient at a representative v is 2Bv, so the singular locus is the projectivization of kerB. Thus the quadric is nonsingular exactly when B is invertible. In the complex projective plane, ranks three, two, and one give respectively a smooth projective conic, two distinct projective lines, and a double projective line.

Canonical form of a quadric (λ1​X12​+⋯+λn​Xn2​+ℓTX+c=0)

Words: 53
Quadric surface OurBigBook.com
The equation of a quadric surface after orthogonal diagonalization of its symmetric matrix and appropriate translation. The spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices removes mixed quadratic terms, and completing squares removes linear terms in directions with nonzero eigenvalues. Linear terms in zero-eigenvalue directions can remain and generate elliptic paraboloids or hyperbolic paraboloids. The signs, zero coefficients and constant distinguish ordinary surfaces, degenerate conics in plane sections, and empty real loci.

Parabolic cylinder (x=c−y2/(4c),c>0)

Words: 50
Quadric surface OurBigBook.com
A quadric surface obtained by extending a parabola along a fixed direction outside its plane. For example, x=c−y2/(4c) with arbitrary z is a parabolic cylinder parallel to the z axis. Each cross-section of fixed z has vertex (c,0) and focus (0,0) in its xy plane. It occurs as a coordinate surface in parabolic cylindrical coordinates.

Distance extrema on a real quadratic surface (xTAx=1,∣x∣2=1/λ)

Words: 163 Articles: 1
Quadric surface OurBigBook.com
For a real symmetric matrix A, every stationary squared distance xTx on xTAx=1 occurs in a positive-eigenvalue eigenspace. The Lagrange multiplier equation is x=ΛAx; multiplying by xT gives Λ=∣x∣2>0, hence Ax=∣x∣−2x. If A is a positive-definite matrix, the nearest and farthest squared distances are 1/λmax​ and 1/λmin​. With a repeated eigenvalue, the stationary set may contain an entire sphere within its eigenspace. For an indefinite or singular form the surface may be unbounded, and a stationary point need not be a global extremum.

Distance extrema on a central plane section of an ellipsoid (dmin2​=λmax​(UTAU)−1,dmax2​=λmin​(UTAU)−1)

Words: 79
Distance extrema on a real quadratic surface OurBigBook.com
Let A be a real positive-definite matrix and let the columns of U be an orthonormal basis of a two-dimensional linear subspace in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Points in that central plane are x=Uq, with ∣x∣2=∣q∣2. Restricting the ellipsoid xTAx=1 gives qT(UTAU)q=1. The compressed matrix UTAU is a positive-definite matrix, and its extreme eigenvalues give the distance formulas in the title by the Rayleigh quotient. The two extremal axes are the images under U of the corresponding eigenvectors. This restriction reduces a problem with two Lagrange multipliers to a two-dimensional quadratic form.

Hyperbolic cylinder (u2/a2−v2/b2=1)

Words: 57
Quadric surface OurBigBook.com
For a,b>0, this quadric surface is independent of its third coordinate and is formed by translating a hyperbola along that direction. Its two connected components correspond to u≥a and u≤−a. In elliptic cylindrical coordinates, fixing a generic angular coordinate selects a half-branch of such a cylinder because the signs of both planar coordinates are fixed by that angular value.

Elliptic cylinder (u2/a2+v2/b2=1)

Words: 58
Quadric surface OurBigBook.com
For a,b>0, an elliptic cylinder is a quadric surface with the displayed equation in suitable Cartesian coordinates, independent of the third coordinate. It is formed by translating an ellipse parallel to a line perpendicular to its plane. The generator direction is the zero-eigenvalue direction of its quadratic part, while the transverse semiaxes are a,b. It is circular if a=b.

Signature transition from an ellipsoid to an elliptic cylinder and a one-sheet hyperboloid (Au2+Bv2+Cw2=1,A,B>0)

Words: 82
Quadric surface OurBigBook.com
After an orthogonal diagonalization, the sign of the third coefficient classifies the displayed quadric surface. If C>0, it is an ellipsoid with semiaxes A−1/2,B−1/2,C−1/2. If C=0, it is an elliptic cylinder parallel to the w axis, with elliptical transverse section. If C<0, it is a one-sheet hyperboloid with axis w and waist ellipse Au2+Bv2=1. The continuous limit C→0 sends the associated axial length scale to infinity. Repeated positive eigenvalues make the corresponding principal-axis choices nonunique within their eigenspace, without changing the surface.

Elliptic cone (au2=bv2+cw2,a,b,c>0)

Words: 66
Quadric surface OurBigBook.com
An elliptic cone is a real quadric surface consisting of the two nappes u=±(bv2+cw2)/a​, joined at the vertex. Its intersections with planes u=u0​=0 are ellipses. It is the zero level of an indefinite quadratic form of signature (1,2). Changing the level to a positive value produces a two-sheeted hyperboloid; changing it to a negative value produces a one-sheet hyperboloid, when the positive coefficient is assigned to the axial coordinate u.

Center (geometry, c)

Words: 52
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
The center of a circle or sphere is the unique point c at the fixed positive radius R from every point of that circle or sphere. In Cartesian coordinates, its equation is ∣x−c∣2=R2. Pythagorean theorem (a2+b2=c2)

Words: 610 Articles: 6
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
For a right triangle in Euclidean geometry with perpendicular side lengths a,b>0 and hypotenuse c, the Pythagorean theorem states
a2+b2=c2.
(11)
Geometrically, the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the other two sides. Euclid's Elements, Book I, Proposition 47 states this area equality; Proposition 48 states its converse: a triangle satisfying the equality has a right angle opposite side c.[ref][ref]
For a=3 and b=4, we compute c=9+16​=5. The triangle has area ab/2=6, and its side lengths form a Pythagorean triple. Conversely, a triangle measured to have sides 3,4,5 must have a right angle between the sides 3 and 4. This makes the equality both a calculation tool and a test for perpendicularity.
The three squares in the next figure have areas 32=9, 42=16 and 52=25 in squared length units. These are different from the central right triangle's area 3⋅4/2=6. The Pythagorean theorem adds the areas of the attached squares, not their side lengths and not the area of the triangle. The square on the hypotenuse is tilted, but a rotation preserves its area. This makes the formula visible without suggesting that the hypotenuse has to align with an axis.
Historically, Euclid's Elements records an organized proof of the Pythagorean theorem as an equality of areas, rather than the modern equation between numbers representing lengths. Its placement in Book I makes it available before the treatment of similar triangles in Book VI. This is evidence of how the result was established within that text; the name Pythagorean theorem alone does not establish who first discovered or proved it. The precise historical anchor here is the surviving proposition, rather than an unsupported story of a single inventor.[ref]
The dissection below makes the general identity tangible. Both outer squares have side a+b and contain the same four congruent right triangles. In the first arrangement, their hypotenuses bound a square of side c: adjacent acute angles together make a right angle. In the second, the uncovered regions are squares of sides a and b. Subtracting the same total triangle area from equal outer areas gives
c2=(a+b)2−42ab​=a2+b2.
(12)
For the pictured dimensions, the shared uncovered area is 49−24=25=9+16.
The same mechanism survives in inner product spaces: for orthogonal vectors u,v, expanding the inner product gives ∥u+v∥2=∥u∥2+∥v∥2. This is why orthogonal projection separates a squared distance into independent contributions. The familiar right triangle is the simplest picture of a much more reusable principle.

Sphere OurBigBook.com

A Euclidean similarity scales both AR​ and R2 by the same factor, so the chosen radius does not affect the answer. On the unit two-sphere, the numerical value is simply the patch's surface area. Unlike an angle drawn in one plane, a solid angle measures coverage in two angular directions.
For example, the full sphere has surface area 4πR2 and hence solid angle 4π steradians. A hemisphere occupies 2π steradians. Three mutually perpendicular coordinate planes divide the directions into eight congruent pieces, so each octant occupies 4π/8=π/2 steradians. A solid angle of one steradian therefore covers 1/(4π)≈7.96% of all directions, rather than one full turn.
This makes a geometric question answer a collection question. For an ideal point emitter with isotropy, equal solid angles carry equal radiant flux. A detector accepting directions of total solid angle Ω intercepts the fraction Ω/(4π) of that emitted radiant flux, before losses. With direction-dependent radiant intensity I, the accepted radiant flux is instead ∫IdΩ. The solid angle of a disk below gives an exact example where the familiar inverse-square law is only a distant-source approximation.

Triangle (△ABC)

Words: 1k Articles: 22
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A triangle is the convex hull of three noncollinear points: the three vertices must not lie on one line. Its boundary consists of the three joining line segments; depending on context, "triangle" can mean this boundary or the filled region it encloses. Here a triangle's area refers to the filled region. The noncollinearity assumption excludes a collapsed shape with zero area, for which ordinary interior angles are not defined.
For example, the positions (0,0), (4,0) and (0,3) form a right triangle with a right angle at the origin. Taking the side of length 4 as its base gives perpendicular height 3, so its area is 4⋅3/2=6. The height is measured at a right angle to the chosen base; it is not generally the length of another side. In this example it happens to be a side because the triangle is a right triangle.
By contrast, side lengths 3,4,6 define a valid triangle: each side is shorter than the sum of the other two, as required by the strict triangle inequality. But 32+42=25=36=62, so this is not a right triangle and the Pythagorean theorem cannot calculate its longest side from the other two. The law of cosines instead gives the opposite interior angle C through
cosC=2⋅3⋅432+42−62​=−2411​,C≈117.28∘.
(24)
This example separates the definition of a triangle from the additional assumption of a right angle.
Every triangle in the Euclidean plane has interior angles summing to π radians, a result proved in Euclid's Elements I.32.[ref] It lets two measured angles determine the third, and underlies the angle-angle criterion for similar triangles. The qualification "Euclidean plane" matters: the earlier spherical triangle demonstrates a different sum.

Triangle OurBigBook.com
Two triangles are similar if a Euclidean similarity maps one onto the other. Their corresponding angles agree, and corresponding side lengths have a common positive ratio.
Specify the correspondence first: A matches A′, B matches B′ and C matches C′. For similar triangles, the common scale factor k>0 satisfies
∣AB∣∣A′B′∣​=∣BC∣∣B′C′∣​=∣CA∣∣C′A′∣​=k.
(25)
The ratios compare matching sides in the same order. A Euclidean similarity can also move, turn or reflect the triangle; its orientation on the page is irrelevant. In the Euclidean plane, matching just two interior angles is enough: their sums force the third to match, and equal corresponding angles force the side ratios to agree. This is the angle-angle (AA) criterion for similar triangles. Matching just one angle is insufficient.
Scale the right triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0) and (0,3) by k=2. Its new vertices are (0,0), (8,0) and (0,6), and its side lengths are 6,8,10. The matching side ratios are 6/3=8/4=10/5=2. Both triangles have a right angle and the same two other interior angles, approximately 36.87∘ and 53.13∘. However, their areas are 3⋅4/2=6 and 6⋅8/2=24: doubling lengths multiplies area by four.
Generally, a Euclidean similarity multiplies both a base and its perpendicular height by k, so the area becomes 21​(kb)(kh)=k221​bh. This explains why an enlarged drawing needs four times as much surface when each length doubles. It also enables indirect measurement: under assumptions of level ground, vertical objects and parallel light rays, an object of height 3 casting a shadow of length 4 provides a right triangle. Another object's shadow of length 8 gives a similar triangle and height 3(8/4)=6. The shared angles justify the inference; visual resemblance alone does not.
Euclid's Elements VI, Definition 1 describes similarity using corresponding angles and proportional sides. VI.4 establishes the implication from matching angles to matching side ratios, while VI.19 states the squared relation between side ratios and areas. These are documented ancient formulations of the principles used above, without establishing a first discoverer.[ref][ref][ref]

Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A conic section is obtained by intersecting a plane with a double circular cone. Cuts away from the vertex produce an ellipse, a parabola or a hyperbola; a perpendicular cut is the circle case of an ellipse. A cut through the vertex can instead produce a degenerate conic. One simple surface therefore connects several familiar plane curves.[ref]
Consider the original family
z2=x2+y2,z=1+mx.
(28)
Substituting the plane equation into the double circular cone equation gives
(1−m2)x2+y2−2mx−1=0.
(29)
Thus m=0 gives a circle, m=3/5 an ellipse, m=1 a parabola, and m=7/5 a hyperbola. The last cut meets both sheets of the double circular cone, producing its two branches. These parameters specify a mathematical family, rather than measurements of a physical object.
The Cartesian coordinate system descriptions of these curves are second-degree equations
Ax2+Bxy+Cy2+Dx+Ey+F=0.
(30)
A rotation and a translation expose their principal directions and offsets. The conic type discriminant identifies the ordinary nondegenerate real type, while a separate degenerate conic check prevents confusing two crossing straight lines with a hyperbola.
This is useful because a difficult-looking equation can be understood through a small set of geometric features: foci of a conic, directrices of a conic, eccentricity of a conic and the semi-major and semi-minor axes. The same ellipse can be traced by a constant-length string or parametrized by x=acost, y=bsint. These are different descriptions of one curve, with different advantages for construction and calculation.

Composing this with the frame change yields the displayed simultaneous congruence of the symmetric coefficient matrices. For nonparallel directions b1​,b2​ and points a1​,a2​, let s1​,s2​ be the independent line parameters at the closest points. Put Δ=a2​−a1​ and D=∣b1​×b2​∣2>0. Perpendicularity of the connecting vector to both directions gives a two-by-two linear system. Solving it and subtracting yields
s2​−s1​=−DΔ⋅[(b1​×b2​)×(b1​−b2​)]​.
(43)
Particles with positions aj​+bj​(t−tj​) reach these two points simultaneously exactly when t1​−t2​=s2​−s1​. Otherwise, their closest approach of two uniformly moving particles can exceed the geometric line distance. The formula requires nonparallel directions; it is not an identity obeyed by arbitrary fixed starting times.

Circles of Apollonius

Words: 28
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
An Apollonius circle is the locus of points whose distances from two fixed points have a prescribed positive ratio different from one. Ratio one gives the perpendicular bisector.

Right angle

Words: 24
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A right angle is an angle of π/2 radians; two nonzero vectors meet at a right angle exactly when their inner product is zero.

Rigid transformation

Words: 96 Articles: 3
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A rigid motion preserves Euclidean distances and therefore preserves angles, lengths, and curvatures.

Rigid-body transformation (x↦Rx+t,RTR=I,detR=1)

Words: 24
Rigid transformation OurBigBook.com
An orientation-preserving rigid transformation, composed of a proper rotation and a translation. This solid-modelling convention distinguishes continuous rigid motion from orientation-reversing distance-preserving maps such as a reflection.

Point reflection

Words: 59 Articles: 1
Rigid transformation OurBigBook.com

Center of symmetry (S=2c−S)

Words: 59
Point reflection OurBigBook.com
A point c is a center of symmetry of a set S in Euclidean space if point reflection x↦2c−x maps S onto itself. Every ellipse has its center of an ellipse as a center of symmetry. More generally, a nonempty bounded set has at most one: two such reflections compose to translation by twice the difference of their centers, and iterating a nonzero translation contradicts boundedness.

Thales's theorem

Words: 25
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
An angle subtended by a diameter of a circle is right; conversely, the hypotenuse of a right triangle inscribed in a circle is a diameter.

Regular polygon

Words: 264 Articles: 3
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A regular polygon has equal side lengths and equal interior angles. Its vertices on a circle are scaled and rotated roots of unity.

Regular heptagon (n=7)

Words: 71
Regular polygon OurBigBook.com
A regular heptagon is a regular polygon with seven sides. Its unit-circle vertices have complex coordinates e2πik/7 for k=0,…,6. It cannot be constructed from a unit segment by a straightedge and compass construction: the first coordinate cos(2π/7) has degree three over Q, since the seventh cyclotomic field has degree six and degree two over its real subfield. Every finite constructible coordinate extension has power-of-two degree, which cannot contain a degree-three subextension by the tower law.

Regular polygon edge rotation criterion (ej+1​=R±2π/n​ej​)

Words: 160
Regular polygon OurBigBook.com
For n≥3 cyclically ordered planar vertices, let ej​=vj+1​−vj​, with indices modulo n. They describe a convex regular polygon exactly when e0​=0 and there is a single choice of sign for which every successive edge vector is obtained by a rotation through 2π/n in that orientation. Necessity follows from equal sides and equal exterior angles. Conversely, the edge vectors have the form Rje0​. Their sum is zero because the corresponding geometric series runs through the n distinct roots of unity. Summing its partial series shows that the vertices are a translated and scaled copy of those roots, so they form a convex regular polygon. A larger turn such as 4π/5 can instead trace a star, which is why merely checking a constant turning angle is insufficient.

Area of a regular octagon

Words: 10
Regular polygon OurBigBook.com
A regular octagon of side length s has area 2(1+sqrt(2))s^2.

Spherical cap

Words: 267 Articles: 4
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A spherical cap is the part of a sphere cut off by a plane.

Mass of a spherical cap with height-proportional density (M=4πk​(R2−c2)2)

Words: 53
Spherical cap OurBigBook.com
For a solid spherical cap r2+z2≤R2, z≥c, where 0≤c≤R and the mass density is ρ=kz with k≥0, a volume integral in cylindrical coordinates gives
M=πk∫cR​z(R2−z2)dz=4πk​(R2−c2)2.
(44)
Here the height is measured from the centre of the sphere, rather than from the bottom of the cap. Specifying that origin matters for a nonuniform mass density.

Curved area of a spherical cap (A=2πRh)

Words: 66
Spherical cap OurBigBook.com
For a sphere of radius R>0, the spherical cap above z=R−h, with 0≤h≤2R, has curved surface area 2πRh. On the surface use r(z)=R2−z2​. The surface of revolution area element is 2πr1+(dr/dz)2​dz=2πRdz. Integrating from R−h to R proves the formula. It includes only the spherical surface; if the planar closing disk is required, add π(2Rh−h2). The coordinate expression is interpreted by a limit at a pole.

Volume of a spherical cap (V=πh2(R−h/3))

Words: 85
Spherical cap OurBigBook.com
For a solid spherical cap of height 0≤h≤2R cut from a sphere of radius R,
V=πh2(R−3h​).​
(45)
Centre the sphere at the origin with the cap on the side z≥R−h. Its cross-section at height z is a circle of squared radius R2−z2. A volume integral in cylindrical coordinates gives
V=∫R−hR​∫02π​∫0R2−z2​​rdrdϕdz=π∫R−hR​(R2−z2)dz=πh2(R−h/3).
(46)
The formula includes caps larger than a hemisphere, when h>R, and the whole solid sphere, when h=2R. For the retained region z≥−d with 0<d<R, set h=R+d to obtain V=π(2R3/3+R2d−d3/3). Multiplying by uniform mass density gives its mass.

Spherical cap area upper bound (Voln−1​(Dρ​)≤sn−1​sinnρ)

Words: 49
Spherical cap OurBigBook.com
On the unit sphere Sn−1, let Dρ​ be a spherical cap of angular radius 0<ρ<π/2. If sinρ≥1/n​, its surface area is at most sn−1​sinnρ. This includes ρ≥π/4 for every n≥2. The bound follows by comparing the cap-area derivative with the derivative of sinnρ and checking the two endpoint values.

Lattice polygon

Words: 18
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
A lattice polygon has all vertices in the integer lattice; triangulation shows that its area is a half-integer.

Isoperimetric inequality

Words: 314 Articles: 4
Euclidean geometry OurBigBook.com
The isoperimetric inequality bounds enclosed volume in terms of boundary size. In the plane it gives 4πA≤L2, with equality for disks; higher-dimensional forms bound the boundary area of a region of prescribed volume.

Planar isoperimetric inequality

Words: 280 Articles: 3
Isoperimetric inequality OurBigBook.com
This is the planar case of the isoperimetric inequality. Every bounded planar domain with a sufficiently regular boundary of length L and area A satisfies
4πA≤L2.
(47)
Equality holds exactly for circular domains.

Maximum-area circular segment with fixed arc length and chord (R=a/sinθ,l/a=θ/sinθ,Amax​=R2(θ−sinθcosθ))

Words: 168
Planar isoperimetric inequality OurBigBook.com
Fix two attachments a distance 2a apart on a straight line and a simple fence of length 2l in one half-plane, with a<l<πa/2. There is a unique θ∈(0,π/2) satisfying l/a=θ/sinθ: its derivative has numerator sinθ−θcosθ>0, since that numerator starts at zero and has derivative θsinθ>0. A radius-R minor circular arc with half-angle θ then has the required chord and length. Its graph is y=R2−x2​−R2−a2​, for −a≤x≤a, and sector-minus-triangle geometry gives the displayed area.
To prove global maximality, attach the complementary major arc of this circle, lying in the opposite half-plane, to any competing fence. The resulting closed curve has perimeter 2l+(2πR−2l)=2πR. Its enclosed area is the competitor's area plus a fixed major-segment area. The planar isoperimetric inequality bounds the total by πR2, with equality only for a circle. Subtracting that fixed added area proves the minor arc is the unique maximizing shape on the chosen side. The same arc follows from the Beltrami identity for the area-minus-length functional.

Hurwitz proof of the planar isoperimetric inequality

Words: 45
Planar isoperimetric inequality OurBigBook.com
Parametrize a positively oriented closed plane curve at constant arc length speed on [0,2π], and let cn​ be its complex-position Fourier coefficients. Green's theorem and Parseval's identity give A=π∑n​n∣cn​∣2 and L2/(4π2)=∑n​n2∣cn​∣2. Since n≤n2 for integers, the planar isoperimetric inequality follows. Equality leaves only the constant and positive first harmonic, a translated circle.

Circle equality in the planar isoperimetric inequality

Words: 34
Planar isoperimetric inequality OurBigBook.com
Equality in the Cauchy-Schwarz and periodic Wirtinger bounds makes the arclength boundary parametrization a first harmonic with orthogonal equal-length coefficient vectors. The boundary is therefore a circle, and the enclosed domain is a disc.
